To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the best response dynamics is a fast and simple method to compute equilibria in combinatorial auctions with item bidding, that the dynamics converges to an equilibrium, and that the dynamics is a good predictor of the outcome of a simultaneous auction.

(1) the dynamics of best response in item bidding auctions is very slow; (2) in the limit of large numbers of bidders, the dynamics is very fast; and (3) the dynamics is fast in the limit of small numbers of bidders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the impact of the bidding strategy on the welfare of the auction?
the following questions:  • How can we model agents' strategies and their interactions in item bidding auctions?
the following questions: 1) How do agents learn to bid in such a game?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
item bidding can lead to high welfare and that it is a promising mechanism.
the welfare at equilibrium is high but the computational complexity of equilibria is high.
the equilibrium is not the right solution concept for item bidding auctions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the equilibrium is indeed hard to compute, but the best-response dynamics can be computed efficiently and lead to high-welfare outcomes.
we show that the dynamics are not as pessimistic as previously thought.
the best-response dynamics is a reasonable approximation for the equilibria of the combinatorial auctions with item bidding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
best-response dynamics are not only computationally tractable, but also converge to high welfare.
best response dynamics can be used to efficiently find high welfare equilibria.
best-response dynamics are not a good way of approximating equilibria in this domain, and therefore equilibrium results are of little practical value.
